title: Circuit Construction & Assembly Methods
description: Commercial circuit assembly — surface mount technology (SMT), through-hole construction, and manual soldering —.
content_html:
From PCB to Finished Circuit

Producing the bare PCB is only the first half of circuit manufacture. The second half is circuit assembly — mounting components onto the board and creating reliable electrical connections between them. The OCR specification identifies three assembly methods: surface mount technology (SMT), through-hole construction, and manual soldering. Each has distinct characteristics, advantages, and disadvantages, and the right choice depends on the scale of production, the components used, and the application.

Surface Mount Technology (SMT)

Surface mount technology (SMT) is the dominant method in modern commercial electronics manufacture. SMT components have no wire leads — instead, they have small metal terminations on their bodies that sit directly on copper pads on the surface of the PCB. Two automated processes are used: first, solder paste (a mixture of tiny solder particles and flux) is printed onto the pads using a stencil. Then, a pick and place machine uses vacuum nozzles to pick individual components from reels or trays at high speed and place them precisely onto the solder paste. Replace 'this is called reflow soldering' with 'this is called reflow soldering' SMT allows very compact circuit layouts (components are much smaller than through-hole equivalents), very high assembly speeds, and both sides of a PCB to be populated. The disadvantages are that SMT components are extremely small and difficult to handle or solder by hand; specialised, expensive equipment is required; and reworking or replacing individual components is more challenging than with through-hole parts.

Key Fact

SMT assembly has two automated stages: (1) pick and place — a robotic machine places tiny components onto solder paste printed on the PCB pads; Replace '(2) reflow soldering — the board passes through a reflow oven' with '(2) reflow soldering — the board passes through a reflow oven' SMT advantage: very compact, fast, suited to mass production. SMT disadvantage: components are too small to solder by hand; expensive automated equipment is required.

Through-Hole Construction

Through-hole construction uses components with wire leads that are pushed through holes drilled in the PCB and soldered to copper pads on the underside. Through-hole components are physically larger than SMT equivalents and create mechanically very strong joints — the lead passing through the board provides a physical anchor. This makes through-hole construction suitable for components that experience mechanical stress, vibration, or repeated connection/disconnection — for example, connectors, power transistors, large capacitors, and switches. Through-hole assembly is also far easier to carry out by hand, making it the standard approach in schools, repair workshops, and for prototyping. The disadvantages are that the holes occupy board space on both layers, limiting routing density, and the components are bulkier, preventing the same miniaturisation achievable with SMT.

Modern commercial electronics predominantly use SMT because the small component size allows smartphones, laptops, and wearables to be as compact as they are. However, through-hole components are still found even on modern PCBs — particularly for connectors (USB ports, power sockets), high-power components (large electrolytic capacitors, power MOSFETs), and mechanical mounting points that benefit from a physically anchored joint. A PCB that uses both SMT and through-hole components is called a mixed-technology board. For the OCR exam, always compare the two based on size, mechanical strength, ease of manual assembly, and suitability for mass production.

Manual Soldering

Manual soldering involves a technician using a soldering iron (typically heated to between 320°C and 380°C) and solder wire to join component leads to PCB pads by hand. The iron tip heats both the component lead and the pad simultaneously; solder wire is then fed into the joint, melts, and flows around the heated surfaces. When the iron is removed, the solder cools and solidifies, creating both an electrical and a mechanical connection. A good solder joint is shiny, smooth, and volcano-shaped. A poor joint — called a cold (dry) joint — is dull, grainy, and has high resistance. Manual soldering is used for through-hole prototyping, repair work, and assembly of low-volume or bespoke circuits. It is unsuitable for SMT components at the normal production scale because the components are too small and the process is too slow for mass manufacture. Safety: the iron tip reaches temperatures that cause immediate burns — always use a stand, avoid touching the tip, and work in a ventilated area to avoid inhaling flux fumes.

Key Fact

Three assembly methods: SMT (tiny surface-mounted components, pick-and-place + reflow oven, mass production — but expensive equipment and difficult to hand-solder); through-hole (leads through drilled holes, strong mechanical joint, easy to hand-solder — but larger components, less dense layout); manual soldering (hand-applied with soldering iron, used for prototypes and repairs — but slow, requires skill, unsuitable for SMT at scale).

A good solder joint must be electrically conductive, mechanically secure, and resistant to fracture in use. In practice, a well-made through-hole joint should be shiny (indicating the solder flowed and bonded correctly), smooth, and volcano-shaped — broader at the pad and tapering up the component lead. A cold joint forms when the pad or lead is insufficiently heated before solder is applied; the solder solidifies before flowing properly, leaving a dull, crumbly surface and a high-resistance connection that may fail intermittently. Other defects include solder bridges (solder accidentally connecting two adjacent pads, causing a short circuit) and insufficient solder (leaving a weak joint). Visual inspection under magnification is the primary quality check for manual soldering in a workshop environment.
exam_tip_html: Questions on assembly methods often ask you to 'compare' or 'justify' a choice for a given production scenario. The key contrasts to memorise are: SMT — tiny components, automated, fast, mass production, but needs expensive machinery and cannot easily be done by hand; through-hole — larger, mechanically strong, easy to hand-solder, but uses more board space; manual soldering — flexible, low cost, used for prototypes and repairs, but slow and reliant on operator skill. For a 6-mark discuss question, always argue both sides and link your conclusion to the specific scenario — scale of production, type of components, and whether automation is available are the deciding factors.

  • Through-hole construction threads component leads through drilled holes and solders them on the underside — the joints are strong and easy to make by hand, but the components are larger and use more board space.
  • Manual soldering with a heated iron is used for prototyping, repairs, and low-volume assembly of through-hole components; a good joint is shiny and smooth, while a cold (dry) joint is dull, grainy, and electrically unreliable.

glossary_terms.definition: The process of attaching and soldering electronic components onto a PCB to create a complete, functional circuit.
A method of circuit assembly in which very small components are placed directly onto pads on the PCB surface and soldered without leads passing through the board.
An automated robotic machine that picks individual SMT components from reels or trays and places them accurately onto solder paste-coated PCB pads at high speed.
A circuit assembly method in which component leads are passed through holes drilled in the PCB and soldered to copper pads on the opposite side.

practice_questions.text:
Which assembly method uses a pick and place machine to position components onto solder paste before reflow soldering in a reflow oven?
A) Manual soldering
B) Through-hole construction
C) Surface mount technology (SMT)
D) Photo etching
State two advantages of through-hole construction compared with surface mount technology (SMT).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: components can be soldered by hand without specialist equipment / through-hole joints are mechanically stronger because the lead passes through the board / easier to repair or replace individual components / through-hole components are larger and easier to handle / suitable for components subject to mechanical stress or vibration. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a 'cold joint' in manual soldering and why it is a problem.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'a cold joint is a bad solder joint'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'a cold joint forms when the component lead or pad is not heated enough before solder is applied, so the solder solidifies before it can flow properly'). A further developed point scores 3 marks (e.g. adding 'the resulting joint is dull and grainy in appearance and has higher electrical resistance than a good joint, which can cause the circuit to fail intermittently or not work at all — it is difficult to detect without close visual inspection or testing under load'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the pick and place stage of surface mount technology (SMT) assembly and explain why it is used in commercial production rather than hand-placing components.
practice_questions.marks: Description of pick and place (up to 2 marks): a robotic machine uses vacuum nozzles to pick individual SMT components from reels or trays and places them precisely onto the solder paste that has been printed onto the PCB pads; the machine operates at very high speed, placing hundreds or thousands of components per hour with consistent accuracy (2 marks for a full, correct description; 1 mark for a basic statement). Reason for use over hand-placing (up to 2 marks): SMT components are extremely small — often only a fraction of a millimetre — making them impossible to place by hand with the accuracy and speed required for commercial production; a pick and place machine achieves consistent placement accuracy across every board in a production run (2 marks for a specific, developed reason; 1 mark for a vague statement such as 'components are too small'). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A company is producing 50,000 units of a compact wireless sensor. A second company is producing a batch of 20 custom audio amplifiers for a music studio. Both need a PCB assembly method.

Discuss which assembly method would be most suitable for each company, giving reasons for your choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion that recommends SMT for the 50,000-unit wireless sensor (justifying with: automated pick and place and reflow soldering allow high-speed, consistent production; SMT components produce compact boards suited to a small wireless sensor; cost per unit is lower at scale) and manual/through-hole for the 20 custom audio amplifiers (justifying with: low volume makes automated SMT equipment uneconomical; through-hole components are easier to hand-solder; audio amplifiers often use large capacitors and power transistors that benefit from through-hole's mechanical strength). Acknowledges trade-offs for both. Conclusions linked clearly to the scenarios.
Secure (3-4 marks): Correct method identified for each scenario with some justification.
Developing (2 marks): One scenario addressed with a basic reason.
Emerging (1 mark): A method named with no justification. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which surface mount technology (SMT) is the most suitable circuit assembly method for all types of electronics manufacture.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies clear strengths of SMT (highly compact boards, fast automated production, both sides of PCB populated, dominant in consumer electronics at scale) and then challenges these with well-developed limitations where SMT is less suitable (requires expensive pick and place and reflow equipment; not viable for low-volume or one-off production; SMT components cannot be easily hand-soldered or repaired; through-hole or manual soldering are more practical for prototyping, repair, education, and components under mechanical stress). The response uses at least two contrasting scenarios and reaches a substantiated conclusion that SMT is not suitable for all types — its advantages are specific to high-volume automated production. Judgement is clearly stated.
Secure (5-6 marks): Strengths and limitations identified with some comparison and a partial judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points listed but limited comparison; no clear judgement.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic description of SMT with little evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What does the pick and place machine do during SMT assembly?
options: It drills holes through the PCB for through-hole components
It picks SMT components from reels and places them onto solder paste on the PCB pads
It applies solder paste to the PCB pads using a stencil
It heats the PCB in a reflow oven to melt the solder paste

knowledge_checks.q: Which assembly method produces the strongest mechanical joint because the component lead physically passes through the board?
A cold (dry) solder joint appears _____ and grainy rather than shiny and smooth, indicating the joint was formed incorrectly.
SMT components are soldered by passing the assembled board through a _____ oven, which melts the solder paste to form solid joints.
Match each assembly method to its most accurate description.
right: A technician uses a heated iron and solder wire to join component leads to pads by hand
Component leads are passed through drilled holes and soldered on the underside of the PCB
Tiny components placed on surface pads by a robotic machine; joints formed in a reflow oven

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between through-hole and surface mount component mounting?
flashcard_questions.a: Through-hole components have wire leads that pass through holes in the PCB; surface mount components sit directly on copper pads on the board surface.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the two automated stages of SMT assembly in the correct order.
flashcard_questions.a: Replace 'reflow soldering in a reflow oven' with 'reflow soldering in a reflow oven'

flashcard_questions.q: What is a pick and place machine?
flashcard_questions.a: A pick and place machine is a robotic system that uses vacuum nozzles to pick SMT components from reels and place them precisely onto PCB pads at high speed.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is SMT unsuitable for manual assembly by hand?
flashcard_questions.a: SMT components are extremely small — often under one millimetre — making them impossible to handle and solder accurately without automated equipment.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one reason why through-hole construction is still used for some components on modern PCBs.
flashcard_questions.a: Through-hole joints are mechanically stronger than SMT joints, making them suitable for connectors and large components that experience physical stress or vibration.

flashcard_questions.q: What temperature range does a soldering iron typically operate at for manual soldering?
flashcard_questions.a: A soldering iron for manual work is typically set between 320°C and 380°C — hot enough to melt solder wire quickly without overheating components.

flashcard_questions.q: Describe the appearance of a good solder joint.
flashcard_questions.a: A good solder joint is shiny, smooth, and volcano-shaped — broader at the PCB pad and tapering up the component lead with a consistent surface finish.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a cold (dry) solder joint and why is it a problem?
flashcard_questions.a: A cold joint is a poorly formed joint where solder did not flow correctly; it is dull and grainy in appearance and has high resistance, causing circuit faults.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a solder bridge and what fault does it cause?
flashcard_questions.a: A solder bridge is an unintended blob of solder joining two adjacent PCB pads, creating a short circuit between the two connections.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is manual soldering unsuitable for large-scale SMT production?
flashcard_questions.a: Manual soldering is far too slow and imprecise for the millions of tiny SMT joints required in commercial production; automated reflow is used instead.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one safety rule for using a soldering iron?
flashcard_questions.a: Always return the iron to its stand when not in use, as the tip reaches temperatures above 350°C and will cause immediate burns if touched accidentally.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of production is manual through-hole soldering most suitable for?
flashcard_questions.a: Manual through-hole soldering is most suitable for prototyping, repair work, and small-batch or bespoke assembly where automated equipment is not available.
